name: Lahu Shi (Retired)
world_status: statement found in an open source

earlier_scan.note: Retired ISO code (split into Kucong lkc and Lahu Shi lhi, 2008); bookkeeping entry, no sources of its own

new_statements.quote: This dialect shows a simple phonemic system, having 23 single consonants ... 8 vowels of two series: oral and laryngealized ... and 5 tonemes: high level, mid level, low level, rising and falling. ... Syllable structure is always CV or CVV with a toneme. ... Tonal change occurs quite frequently: a sequence of two high tones results in that of low and high tones. The language seems to be following the similar process of changing from a syllabic-tone type to a quasi word-tone type as seen in the Akha language, although the latter has more clearly a feature of stress. (See T. Nishida, "A preliminary report on the Akha language," Studia Phonologica, IV 1965/66.)
new_statements.citation: Nishida, Tatsuo. 1969. ラフ・シ語の研究: タイ国チェンライ県におけるラフ・シ族の言葉の予備報告 [A Preliminary Study on the Lahu Shi Language in Chiang Rai Province]. 東南アジア研究 (Southeast Asian Studies, Kyoto) 7(1): 2-39.
new_statements.locator: English summary, p. 2 (PDF p. 1); tone system detailed in Japanese in the 声調 subsection, pp. 8-10
new_statements.second_reader_evidence: QUOTE: Opened (38 pp., text layer present, no scanned). The quoted passage is on the English summary page (journal p. 2 = PDF p. 1) exactly as reported; the ellipses only elide the consonant/vowel phoneme lists, and the text layer has trivial scanned glitches ('simp]e', 'vowers') that do not affect the wording. Verbatim: '.. 5 tonemes: high level, mid level, low level, rising and falling.. Syllable structure is always CV or CVV with a toneme.. Tonal change occurs quite frequently: a sequence of two high tones results in that of low and high tones. The language seems to be following the similar process of changing from a syllabic-tone type to a quasi word-tone type as seen in the Akha langua…
new_statements.rule_in_words: Lahu Shi (Yellow Lahu of Mae Chan, Chiang Rai) is described as a syllable-tone language: every CV(V) syllable bears one of five tonemes; there is productive tone sandhi (H+H -> L+H) which the author reads as incipient drift toward a word-tone type, but unlike Akha, Lahu Shi is said not to show a clear stress feature. No position of word stress is stated; stress is not set up as a phonological category.
new_statements.exceptions: Only the tone-sandhi rule (two high tones -> low + high); gliding tonemes have high allotones on laryngealized vowels and low allotones on oral vowels.
new_statements.domain_note: Statement is about the tonal typology of the word (syllable-tone vs quasi word-tone); based on one female speaker, elicited through Burmese, 1964 fieldwork. The description is of Lahu Shi proper, i.e. Glottolog lahu1252 [lhi], one of the two successors of the retired code.
new_statements.first_reading: tone language with a stress statement
new_statements.identity_note: lahu1255 is a Glottolog bookkeeping entry for the retired ISO 639-3 code [kds] 'Lahu Shi', split on 2008-01-14 (CR 2007-090) into Lahu Shi [lhi] = lahu1252 (Yellow Lahu; Thailand/Myanmar/Laos/China) and Kucong [lkc] = kuco1235 (Yunnan, Vietnam). It has no descriptive literature of its own and, by our rule that each source is filed under the language's current Glottolog code (a retired code does not make a separate language), should not receive a catalog entry. The Nishida 1969 statement quoted here describes Lahu Shi proper (Mae Chan, Chiang Rai, Thailand) and should be filed under lahu1252 — whose earlier our earlier survey classification was no source found — not under lahu1255. Kucong sources (Chang 2011; Dai & Chang 2009) belong under kuco1235.

new_statements.quote: There is, however, a separate pitch assimilation phenomenon which occurs in Banian. Certain syllables, including the productive noun prefix a, the negative adverb (801) ma, and the negative imperative adverb (802) ta, the numerals 'one' (478) te and 'two' (479) ni, and some other first syllables in polysyllabic words, have a pitch which is phonetically similar to the pitch at which the Tone of the following syllable begins. [...] The negative adverbs in Black Lahu and most other dialects are Tone 1 syllables, with the appropriate pitch and contour features, but they are often not stressed.
new_statements.citation: Bradley, David. 1979. Lahu Dialects. Oriental Monograph Series 23. Canberra: Faculty of Asian Studies in association with Australian National University Press. xi+291 pp. (section 'i. Banian', pp. 110-120 = Lahu Shi Banlan phonology).
new_statements.locator: printed p. 119 (PDF p. 142), section 'i. Banian', subsection 'b. phonology' (printed pp. 114-120 = PDF pp. 137-143); tone table printed pp. 116-117 (PDF pp. 139-140): 'The seven Tones in Banian have several alternative realizations which are appropriate to different juncture environments.'
new_statements.second_reader_evidence: Text layer lines 5858-5876 and extracted text of PDF p. 142 (printed '119' at top) contain the quoted passage word for word: 'There is, however, a separate pitch assimilation phenomenon which occurs in Banian. Certain syllables, including the productive noun prefix a, the negative adverb (801) ma, and the negative imperative adverb (802) ta, the numerals "one" (478) te and "two" (479) ni, and some other first syllables in polysyllabic words, have a pitch which is phonetically similar to the pitch at which the Tone of the following syllable begins.' and after the three-line assimilation table and the Black Lahu a-prefix remark: 'The negative adverbs in Black Lahu and most other dialects are…
new_statements.relation_note: Compatible with the existing Nishida 1969 statement (tone language, no stress statement) and adds detail: seven tones rather than Nishida's five tonemes, juncture-conditioned allotones, absence of Black Lahu tone sandhi, and a class of pitch-assimilating weak first syllables (prefixes, negators, low numerals); still no word-stress placement. Bradley states (p. 110, 119-120) this is the same Banian variety Nishida, Matisoff and Dellinger recorded in Thailand, so it belongs under lahu1252.
new_statements.rule_in_words: Banian (Lahu Shi Banlan) is described as a seven-tone language whose tones have juncture-conditioned allotones (word-medial, word-final, clause/sentence-final); no word-stress rule or stress placement is stated anywhere in the section, and 'stress' occurs once in the whole book. The only stress remark says negative adverbs in Black Lahu and most other dialects carry Tone 1 'but they are often not stressed'. For Banian itself the analogous fact is pitch assimilation: prefixes, negative adverbs, numerals 'one'/'two' and some other first syllables of polysyllabic words take a pitch copied from the onset of the following syllable's tone, i.e. they behave as weak, tonally dependent syllables.
new_statements.exceptions: Pitch-assimilating syllables listed: noun prefix a, negative adverb ma, negative imperative ta, numerals te 'one', ni 'two', and some other first syllables in polysyllabic words (pp. 119). No Black-Lahu-style tone sandhi in Banian (p. 119). Laos subdialect has Tone 7 mid level (p. 117). Matisoff proposed eight tones, Dellinger six; Bradley keeps seven (p. 117).
new_statements.identity_note: lahu1255 is a Glottolog bookkeeping key for the retired ISO code kds (split 2008-01-14 into Lahu Shi lhi = lahu1252 and Kucong lkc = kuco1235). Both works read here describe Lahu Shi Balan/Banlan ('Banian', Yellow Lahu) as spoken in northern Thailand (Chiang Rai, Chiang Mai; Bradley also notes a Laos subdialect and refugees from Laos), i.e. the successor lahu1252, not Kucong. Any catalog entry built from these belongs under lahu1252; lahu1255 has no literature of its own.

sources.note: Describes Lahu Shi (Yellow Lahu, Mae Chan, Chiang Rai) as a syllable-tone language with 5 tonemes on every CV(V) syllable and frequent tone sandhi (high+high -> low+high); says the language seems to be drifting toward a 'quasi word-tone type' like Akha, but that Akha 'has more clearly a feature of stress' — i.e. no word-stress placement rule is given for Lahu Shi and stress is not treated as a phonological category. Japanese body (声調 section, pp. 8ff.) treats tonemes/allotones only; no 強勢/ストレス/アクセント discussion found in the text layer.
